launcher.placeholder: Type a keyword, e.g. usbipd or "attach"
launcher.prompt: Type a keyword to start searching

language.title: Interface language
language.note: Applies to the launcher, this window, the tray menu and the descriptions of the built-in commands. Following the system means using the Windows display language.

general.shortcutNote: A modifier plus a key code, for example Alt+KeyQ or Control+Shift+Space. Letter keys are written like KeyQ. Avoid Alt+Space — Windows reserves it for the window menu.
general.shortcutFellBack: {{wanted}} could not be registered, most likely because another program has it. {{active}} is what actually works right now; pick a different combination and apply it again.
general.shortcutNoneActive: {{wanted}} could not be registered, so no shortcut opens the launcher at the moment — use the tray icon, or pick a different combination here.

opacity.title: Launcher background
opacity.note: The launcher floats above the window you are working in. Lower opacity lets more of it show through; the background blur keeps the command text readable. The launcher is hidden while this window is open, so the preview below is what it actually looks like.
opacity.minimumHint: Minimum {{percent}}% — any lower and the content underneath makes the commands hard to read.

startup.title: Startup
startup.note: QQKey normally has no visible window; it lives in the tray. Left-click the icon to open the launcher, right-click for the menu.
startup.label: Start automatically at sign-in

history.title: Learning from history
history.note_one: Learns the commands you actually run from your PSReadLine history; the more often one appears, the higher it starts. Imports incrementally, reading only what is new since last time. The pool currently holds {{count}} command.
history.note_other: Learns the commands you actually run from your PSReadLine history; the more often one appears, the higher it starts. Imports incrementally, reading only what is new since last time. The pool currently holds {{count}} commands.
history.report_one: Scanned {{count}} line, imported {{imported}}, skipped {{skippedSecret}} that looked like credentials and {{skippedNoise}} as noise.
history.report_other: Scanned {{count}} lines, imported {{imported}}, skipped {{skippedSecret}} that looked like credentials and {{skippedNoise}} as noise.

secret.title: Credential filter
secret.note: History lines matching this regular expression are skipped entirely — they never reach the database and never appear in the launcher. Only the number of skipped lines is reported; their contents are not recorded. A second, fixed rule also blocks any run of 20 or more characters after = or :, and is not affected by this setting.
secret.warning: Before loosening this: a credential that slips through stays in the local database. A command caught by mistake can simply be added back on the {{tab}} tab.

share.title: Share your commands
share.note: Exchanged as JSON through the clipboard. Only the commands you added or edited yourself — the built-in catalogue is on the other machine too, and anything learnt from history may carry work content, so neither is exported.
share.clipboardEmpty: The file in the clipboard has no commands

backup.title: Backup and restore
backup.note: Not the same thing as {{share}} above. A backup takes everything — built-in entries, whatever was learnt from history, the accumulated usage statistics and every setting on this page — so a new machine can be put back exactly as it was. Those thousands of learnt entries travel no other way.
backup.warning: Restoring replaces all current data, including commands you have added or edited since.
backup.saved_one: Backed up {{count}} command and the current settings
backup.saved_other: Backed up {{count}} commands and the current settings

import.confirm_one: This file holds {{count}} command, and it will be added.
import.confirm_other: This file holds {{count}} commands, all of which will be added.
import.confirmOverwrite_one:
This file holds {{count}} command: adds {{added}}, overwrites {{overwritten}} already here.

The descriptions and keywords that get overwritten are replaced by the versions in the file, and that cannot be undone.
import.confirmOverwrite_other:
This file holds {{count}} commands: adds {{added}}, overwrites {{overwritten}} already here.

{{path}}

This backup will replace all current data — existing commands, usage statistics and settings will all be overwritten, and that cannot be undone.

logs.title: Diagnostic log
logs.note: QQKey normally has no visible window, so when something goes wrong the log is the only way to work out which step failed. It records how far opening the launcher, locating the caret and inserting the text each got, and records neither window titles nor the text that was inserted.

entries.scoreHint: The decayed usage score — the same one the launcher sorts by

entries.deleteManyMessage_one:

entries.deleteManyMessage_other:

entry.templateHint: Mark the parts you fill in yourself with {name}. When inserted, the command is cut off just before the first placeholder, leaving the caret exactly where you take over.
entry.keywordsHint: Separated by spaces. Add words in your own language and you can find this command in that language.
entry.keywordsBuiltinHint: This is a built-in entry, showing the keywords for the current language; once saved it becomes your own entry and only uses what you type here.
entry.boostHint: Added to the frecency score to keep this command near the top. Negative values are not accepted — to keep something out of the launcher, disable it.

about.pitch: Press the shortcut in any window to open the launcher, type a keyword to find a command, and it is inserted into the command line rather than run — with the caret at the first thing you need to fill in. Whether to press Enter is up to you. Frequently used commands rise on their own through frecency.
about.dataValue: Stored entirely on this machine, never sent anywhere
about.origin: QQKey is written and maintained by {{author}} alone. The reason was simple: the subcommands and flags of tools like usbipd, git and netsh would not stick, and every time meant going back to --help. So this is a tool for finding commands by keywords in your own language, which then puts them in the command line for one more look rather than pressing the key for you.
about.contact: Questions, commands worth adding to the built-in catalogue, or bug reports — any of the routes below reaches me.
about.secretWarning: When reporting a problem, please avoid pasting command text that contains credentials or internal paths.
